subject: history
displayName: KS3 History — The Cold War, Decolonisation & Migration
subtitle: Superpower rivalry after 1945, the end of the British Empire, and post-war migration to Britain.

data.targetWord: the period of rivalry after 1945 between the USA and USSR involving threats, propaganda, arms races and proxy wars, but no direct full-scale war between the superpowers

examples.en-GB: The Cold War shaped international politics from 1945 until the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991.

data.targetWord: a country with great military, economic and political influence across the world; after 1945 the USA and USSR were the main superpowers

examples.en-GB: The USA and the USSR were the two superpowers whose rivalry defined the Cold War era.

data.targetWord: an economic and political system based on private ownership of businesses and the right to make profit, championed by the USA during the Cold War

examples.en-GB: The USA promoted capitalism and liberal democracy as alternatives to Soviet communism.

data.targetWord: a political and economic system based on state ownership of resources and one-party rule, as practised in the Soviet Union

examples.en-GB: The USSR promoted communism and feared the spread of capitalism and Western influence.

data.targetWord: a competition between countries to build more powerful weapons; during the Cold War the USA and USSR competed to develop nuclear arsenals

examples.en-GB: The arms race meant both sides possessed enough nuclear weapons to destroy each other many times over.

data.targetWord: a conflict in which superpowers support opposing sides without fighting each other directly

examples.en-GB: The Korean War was a proxy war in which the USA and USSR supported different sides.

data.targetWord: the US foreign policy of trying to prevent the spread of communism to other countries

examples.en-GB: The policy of containment led the USA to intervene in Korea, Vietnam and other parts of the world.

data.targetWord: the Soviet attempt in 1948–49 to cut off Western access to West Berlin by blocking road, rail and canal routes

examples.en-GB: The Berlin Blockade was the first major Cold War crisis in Europe, prompting the Western Airlift.

data.targetWord: the Western Allied operation to fly food, fuel and supplies into West Berlin during the Soviet blockade of 1948–49

examples.en-GB: The Berlin Airlift showed the West's determination to protect West Berlin without starting a war.

data.targetWord: a dangerous 1962 confrontation when the USA discovered Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba, bringing the world close to nuclear war

examples.en-GB: The Cuban Missile Crisis lasted thirteen days and was the closest the Cold War came to nuclear conflict.

data.targetWord: the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, a Western military alliance formed in 1949 to resist Soviet influence in Europe

examples.en-GB: NATO was formed in 1949 following the Berlin Blockade as a collective defence agreement.

data.targetWord: the process by which colonies gained independence from imperial rule, particularly after 1945

examples.en-GB: Decolonisation was driven by anti-colonial movements, economic pressures and changing international opinion.

data.targetWord: when a country governs itself rather than being ruled by another state

examples.en-GB: India achieved independence from Britain in 1947, inspiring many other independence movements.

data.targetWord: the division of a territory into separate states, as when British India was divided into India and Pakistan in 1947

examples.en-GB: Partition in 1947 led to massive migration and communal violence as millions crossed new borders.

data.targetWord: a group of independent countries, many formerly part of the British Empire, that cooperate while remaining self-governing

examples.en-GB: Many Caribbean and African countries joined the Commonwealth after gaining independence from Britain.

data.targetWord: people who migrated from the Caribbean to Britain between 1948 and the early 1970s, named after the ship HMT Empire Windrush which arrived in 1948

examples.en-GB: The Windrush generation contributed enormously to the NHS, transport and public services in post-war Britain.

data.targetWord: a reason that encourages people to leave a place, such as unemployment, conflict or limited opportunities

examples.en-GB: Limited job opportunities in the Caribbean were a push factor that encouraged people to migrate to Britain.

data.targetWord: a reason that attracts people to a particular place, such as available jobs, family connections, safety or education

examples.en-GB: Labour shortages in Britain's NHS and transport services were pull factors that attracted Caribbean migrants.

data.targetWord: a law that gave people from the UK and its colonies shared citizenship status, allowing many Commonwealth citizens legal rights to enter and live in Britain

examples.en-GB: The British Nationality Act 1948 gave Windrush migrants the legal right to live and work in Britain.

data.targetWord: describing a society made up of people from many different cultural, ethnic, religious and national backgrounds

examples.en-GB: Post-war migration transformed Britain into a multicultural society with diverse food, music and religious traditions.

data.targetWord: the leader of Ghana's independence movement who became Ghana's first Prime Minister when Ghana gained independence from Britain in 1957

examples.en-GB: Kwame Nkrumah led Ghana to independence in 1957, inspiring other African independence movements.

data.targetWord: a set of ideas about how society, government and the economy should be organised

examples.en-GB: Ideological differences between capitalism and communism drove the rivalry between the USA and USSR.

data.targetWord: historical evidence based on spoken memories and personal interviews, used to record experiences that may not appear in official documents

examples.en-GB: Oral history interviews with Windrush migrants captured personal experiences of arrival, work and discrimination.

data.targetWord: the Cold War idea that a nuclear war between the superpowers would destroy both sides, making such a war too dangerous to start

examples.en-GB: Mutually assured destruction created a dangerous stability because neither side could win a nuclear war.

data.targetWord: the principle that peoples and nations have the right to govern themselves and choose their own political system

examples.en-GB: The United Nations supported self-determination, lending international legitimacy to independence movements.

data.sentence: The Cold War was a rivalry between the USA and the ____ that lasted from 1945 to 1991.
The ____ of 1948–49 saw the West fly supplies into a blockaded city to resist Soviet pressure.
The ____ in 1962 brought the USA and USSR to the brink of nuclear war over missiles in Cuba.
India and Pakistan became independent from Britain in ____.
____ became the first West African country to gain independence from Britain in 1957.
HMT Empire Windrush arrived at ____ Docks in Essex in June 1948.
A reason that encourages people to leave a place, such as unemployment, is called a ____ factor.
NATO was formed in ____ as a Western military alliance to resist Soviet influence.
A war where superpowers support different sides without fighting each other directly is called a ____ war.
Partition in 1947 involved the division of British India into India and ____.
The British Nationality Act ____ gave many Commonwealth citizens the legal right to enter and live in Britain.
The Soviet Union ____ in 1991, marking the end of the Cold War.
Post-war Caribbean migrants contributed greatly to the ____, working as nurses, doctors and porters.
The Korean War 1950–53 ended in an ____, leaving Korea divided, not a full peace treaty.
Decolonisation was not simply a gift of freedom from Britain — it resulted from anti-colonial ____ and movements.

data.title: Order the key Cold War events chronologically
items: 1945 — Second World War ends; United Nations founded
1949 — NATO formed as Western military alliance
1950–53 — Korean War — a Cold War proxy conflict
1962 — Cuban Missile Crisis brings world close to nuclear war

data.title: Order key decolonisation events from earliest to latest
items: 1947 — India and Pakistan gain independence; partition causes widespread violence
1948 — HMT Empire Windrush arrives at Tilbury with Caribbean migrants
1957 — Ghana becomes independent from Britain under Kwame Nkrumah
1963 — Kenya gains independence after the Mau Mau uprising and British repression

data.title: Order the end of the Cold War events
items: 1979 — Soviet Union invades Afghanistan, reigniting tension
1985 — Mikhail Gorbachev introduces reforms in the USSR
1989 — Berlin Wall is opened as Soviet control weakens
1991 — Soviet Union collapses and Cold War ends
Post-1991 — Former Soviet bloc countries move towards independence and democracy
